en: Śrī Śuka said:
O King, this question you have asked is most excellent, for it is for the welfare of the world;
it is the one among all things to be heard that is esteemed by those who know the Self.
O King of kings, there are thousands of things for men to hear and so forth,
yet they do not perceive the reality of the Self while remaining householders in their homes.
Their youth is stolen away by sleep at night and by sexual indulgence.
O King, whether by the pursuit of wealth during the day or by the maintenance of a family,

one remains intoxicated even while witnessing their own destruction; for though the body, children, wife, and other such things— which constitute the army of the self— are actually non-existent, he does not perceive this.
Therefore, O descendant of Bharata, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign and the Self of all,
should be heard, glorified, and remembered by one who desires fearlessness.
This much is achieved through Sāṅkhya and Yoga, and through steadfastness in one's own duty.

The supreme attainment of birth for men is the remembrance of Nārāyaṇa at the end. O King, for the most part, the sages who have desisted from injunctions and prohibitions abide in the state beyond the modes and delight in the narration of the qualities of Hari.
I studied this Purāṇa named Bhāgavata,

which is equal to the Veda, from my father Dvaipāyana at the beginning of the Dvāpara age; though I was already established in the state beyond the three qualities (nirguṇya), I was captivated by the pastimes of the Lord of Excellent Praise.
O royal sage, since your mind has been captivated, I shall relate to you that narrative which you have studied; for you are a man of great spiritual prowess,
and for those who have faith in it, a steady devotion to Mukunda will quickly arise.

O King, for those yogīs who are weary of worldly existence and desire freedom from all fear, the chanting of the names of Hari has been determined as the certain path. What is the use of many years spent here in negligence regarding things beyond perception?
It is better to know even for a moment that which leads to the highest good;
for the royal sage named Khaṭvāṅga, having realized the limited extent of life here,
abandoned everything after a mere moment and went to the fearless Hari.

O descendant of Kuru, even for you, the limit of life now remains but seven days. Therefore, prepare all those things that are required for the afterlife; for when the time of death has arrived, a person is free from fear.
One should cut away with the weapon of non-attachment the longing for the body and for those who are attached to it.
Having renounced the home, the wise man, bathed in the waters of sacred pilgrimage sites,
sits in a pure and secluded place upon a seat prepared according to rule.
One should practice with the mind the pure, threefold, supreme, imperishable Brahman. Having controlled the breath, one should restrain the mind while not forgetting the seed-syllable of Brahman.
With the intellect as charioteer, one should restrain the senses from their objects by means of the mind.
One should indeed hold with the intellect the mind, which has been drawn away by actions, toward a virtuous object.

There, one should meditate upon even a single limb [of the Lord] with an uninterrupted consciousness. Having yoked the mind so that it is free from sense-objects, one should thereafter not think of anything at all.
That is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, wherein the mind becomes serene.
The wise man should restrain with meditative concentration his own deluded mind, which is agitated by *rajas* and *tamas*; for such concentration destroys the impurity produced by those qualities.
"When this [devotional service] is maintained, the yoga characterized by devotion quickly becomes perfected for the practitioner who beholds the auspicious refuge.
The King said:
"O Brahmin, how is that concentration (dhāraṇā) maintained which is considered approved,
or of what nature is it that quickly removes the impurity of a person's mind?
Śrī Śuka said:
Having mastered his posture, his breath, his attachments, and his senses,
he should fix his mind with his intellect upon the gross form of the Blessed One;
for this body of His is the most massive of all massive things.
In this body,
which is like the shell of the cosmic egg and is endowed with seven coverings,
that very Vairāja Puruṣa— the Blessed Lord who is the support of *dhāraṇā*— is manifested as the reality (*sat*) consisting of the past, the future, and the present.
They declare that Pātāla is the soles of his feet; Rasātala is his heels and forefeet;
Mahātala is the two ankles of the Creator of the universe; and Talātala is indeed the two shanks of that Puruṣa.
Sutala is the two knees of the Universal Form; Vitala and Atala are his two thighs.
O Lord of the Earth, they declare the surface of the earth to be His hips, the vault of the sky to be the lake of His navel,

the host of luminaries to be His chest, the Maharloka to be His neck, and the Janoloka to be His mouth; they know the Tapoloka to be the nose-string of the Primal Person, and the Satyaloka to be the heads of Him who has a thousand heads.
Indra and the other gods are his arms; the sun is his hands; the quarters of space are his ears, and sound is his sense of hearing.
The two Aśvins, Nāsatya and Dasra, are his nostrils; his sense of smell is fragrance; and the blazing fire is his mouth.
The sky is his eyes, and the sun became his sight; both day and night are the eyelashes of Viṣṇu.
The expansion of his eyebrows is the abode of Parameṣṭhin; the waters are his palate, and taste itself is his tongue.
They declare that the Vedic meters are the head of the Infinite One, Yama is his teeth, and the digits of affection are his teeth-sockets.
His smile is the Māyā that maddens the world, and the casting of his sidelong glance is the creation of endless variety.
O King, for this Universal Being, shame is His upper lip, greed is His lower lip; righteousness is His breast, and the path of unrighteousness is His back.
His penis is Kaśyapa, His testicles are the two Aśvins, His belly is the oceans, and the mountains are the collection of His bones.
O Lord of men, the rivers are His veins, and the trees are the hairs on His body.
O best of the Kurus, they know the wind to be the breath of the Infinite One, whose prowess is endless; His movement is time, and the flow of the qualities is His activity.

They know the clouds to be the hair of the Lord, while the twilight is the garment of that All-pervading One. They say the unmanifest is His heart, and the moon is His mind, which is the sheath of all transformations.

They declare His majesty to be the power of consciousness and the inner organ (intellect) of the Self of all; Giritra is His nails; horses, mules, camels, and elephants, as well as all wild animals and domestic cattle, are from the region of His hips;
birds are His diverse speech; Manu is His intelligence, and Manuja is His abode.
He possesses the splendor of the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, Apsarases, Svaras, Smṛtis, and the hosts of Asuras;

he is the mouth of Brahmā, the arms of the Kṣatriyas, the thighs of the Vaiśyas, and the feet of the Śūdras; he is the Great Soul who assumes a dark hue, endowed with various names and the assembly of sacrifices, consisting of ritual materials, and joined with the performance of sacrificial rites.
Such is this configuration of the Lord’s form that has been described by me to you;
one should fix the mind upon this most stable body through one's own intelligence, for there exists nothing else apart from it.
That Self, which is experienced through all the modifications of the intellect, is like the single witness who perceives the people in a dream.
One should worship that Truth, the treasure-house of bliss, and not become attached to anything else, for from such attachment comes the downfall of the self.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus, in the past, the Self-born [Brahmā], having regained his lost memory through meditative concentration, was satisfied.
Thus, with unfailing vision and a resolute intellect, He created this universe just as He had resolved upon it before its dissolution.

For this is the path of the Brahman that consists of sound (śabda-brahman): that the wise man meditates upon it through names that lack external objects. Wandering therein and lying within the realm of illusion due to latent impressions (vāsanā), he does not perceive the true objects.
Therefore, a wise man, being vigilant and possessing a resolute intellect, should apply himself only so far as is necessary regarding names;

he should not strive for that which is already established otherwise, observing the labor involved therein. When the earth is available, what is the use of the effort of making a bed? And when one’s own arm is available, what is the use of pillows?

What need is there for a vessel of various foods when truth itself is in the hollowed palms? What need is there for silk garments when bark-cloths and the like are available? Are there no rags on the road?
Do trees not offer alms, and do the rivers never run dry?
Why does the Unconquered One not protect those who have approached Him, even though He has blocked the caves [of the senses]?
Why do the wise instead worship those blinded by the intoxication of wealth?
Thus, the Lord Ananta—the Self, the beloved goal—is established within one's own mind by His very nature.

One who is at peace and whose purpose is fixed should worship Him, in whom the cause of worldly existence ceases; for who, disregarding that supreme state, would pursue the thought of others—that which is called "unreal"—except for those who are like beasts?
Behold the people fallen into the Vaitaraṇī river, experiencing the torments born of their own karma.
Some meditate through *dhāraṇā* upon the Person dwelling within the space of their own heart, measuring only a span,

possessing four arms and holding a lotus, a discus, a conch, and a mace; He whose face is smiling, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, and who is clothed in garments the color of the filaments of a *kadamba* flower.

He wore golden armlets set with shimmering great jewels and a crown and earrings of glittering great gems; his sprout-like feet were placed by the lords of yoga upon the pericarp of the fully blossomed lotus of the heart; he was marked with the sign of Śrī, bore the Kaustubha jewel upon his neck, and was adorned with a forest garland of unfading splendor.

Adorned with a girdle, costly finger-rings, anklets, bracelets, and other ornaments; his face graced by a gentle smile and beautiful, glossy, stainless, curly black locks of hair; and manifesting great favor through his noble, playful smiles, glances, and the quivering play of his eyebrows.
One should contemplate this Lord, who consists of pure consciousness, for as long as the mind remains steady through concentration.

One should meditate upon the limbs of the wielder of the mace one by one with the intellect, beginning from the feet up to His smile. As the intellect becomes increasingly purified, one should discard each part already mastered and fix the mind upon the next higher part.
As long as the yoga of devotion has not arisen toward this Lord of all, the witness of both the high and the low,
so long should the ascetic, striving at the conclusion of his ritual acts, meditate upon the gross form of the Supreme Person.
O dear one, when the ascetic, established in a steady and comfortable posture, desires to leave this world, [he should do so].

One should not allow the mind to become attached to time or place; having conquered the senses, one should restrain the vital breaths by means of the mind. Having restrained the mind with pure intelligence, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) should lead that mind into the Self.
Having confined the self within the Self, the wise man, having attained tranquility, should desist from all activity.
There, Time—the supreme lord of the unblinking ones—has no power; how then could the gods who rule over the worlds have any?
There, neither goodness, passion, nor darkness exists, nor indeed the transformations, nor the Great Principle (mahat), nor primordial matter (pradhāna).
Those who desire to cast off that which is not the Self declare that supreme state of Viṣṇu to be "not this, not this" (neti neti).
Having cast off all wickedness and with hearts full of exclusive affection, they embrace at every step Him whose feet are worthy of worship.

Thus, the sage who is firmly established in this way—his heart thoroughly perfumed by the power of realized vision—should attain liberation. Then, having pressed his anus with his heel, he who has conquered fatigue should direct the vital air (anila) through the six locations.
Having placed [the breath] situated at the navel into the heart, the sage should lead it from there to the chest by means of the *udāna* breath;
then, having followed it with his intellect, the wise one should slowly lead it to the root of his own palate.
From there, he should lead it to the space between the eyebrows, having restrained the seven sense-bases and become indifferent to all else.
Having remained for half a muhūrta with unblinking vision, he pierces the crown of the head and, having departed, reaches the Supreme.
O King, if one is about to go to the realm of Brahmā (pārameṣṭhya), or to the abode of the celestial beings (vaihāyasa),
or to the sovereignty over the eight [directions] within the assembly of the modes of nature (guṇa-sannivāya), he goes there together with his mind and senses.
They say that the goal of the masters of yoga, whose inner selves are like the wind and who transcend the three worlds both within and without,
is not attained through ritual actions, but by those who possess knowledge, austerity, yoga, and meditative absorption.
Having departed through the *suṣumṇā* nerve, one goes by the path of Brahman, the radiant Vaiśvānara, through the ether.

O King, with his impurities shaken off, he then ascends from the region of Hari to the Śaiśumāra Cakra. Having passed beyond that, which is the navel of the universe, he— alone, by means of the subtle and stainless self of Viṣṇu—
approaches that which is saluted by the knowers of Brahman, where the gods dwell for the duration of a kalpa.
Then, beholding the entire universe being scorched by the fire from the mouth of Ananta,
he departed for that abode of the Lord of Siddhas which lasts for two *parārdhas* and belongs to the Supreme Lord (*pārameṣṭhya*),
where there is no sorrow, no old age, no death, no affliction, and no agitation arising from any source.
Because he perceived that the source of insurmountable suffering for those who lack knowledge arises from that very state, he attained a distinction beyond it through compassion.

Then, becoming fearless, he proceeded by means of that self as water, then as fire, and then as light; having reached the wind at the proper time, he entered the ether through the nature of the wind—the vast ether which is the mark of the Great Self.
Through the sense of smell he perceives fragrance, through the tongue taste, through sight form, and through the skin touch;
through the ear he attains the quality of space (sound), and through the vital breath (prāṇa) the yogi attains consciousness.
He [perceives] the contact between the subtle elements, the senses, and the mind, which consists of the divine and is subject to transformation.
Having reached that state through that path, he goes to the reality of pure consciousness where the qualities (guṇas) are completely restrained.
By means of that self, he attains the peaceful Self, which is bliss; at the end, being composed of bliss, he reaches bliss itself.
O dear one, he who has attained this divine goal does not indeed become attached to this world again.
O King, these two paths, sung of in the Vedas and eternal, have been described by me as you requested;
they are indeed those which the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, when propitiated and pleased, formerly told to Brahmā.
For there is no other auspicious path for one entering into this cycle of worldly existence.
From this, devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) toward Vāsudeva, the Blessed Lord,
arises. Having scrutinized the Blessed Brahman in its entirety three times with his intellect, the immutable Lord determined that from which delight in the Self might arise.
The Blessed Lord Hari is perceived within all beings by means of his own self;
he is the seer, inferred through perceptible characteristics such as the intellect and other faculties.
Therefore, O King, Hari is the Self of all, present everywhere and at all times.
The Blessed Lord should be heard, glorified, and remembered by men. Those who drink the nectar of the discourse of the virtuous concerning the Blessed Self, gathered within the cups of their ears,
purify their hearts defiled by sense objects and go to the vicinity of His lotus feet.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus has been related that which you asked me,
concerning those wise men among humanity who are about to die.
One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should worship Brahmaṇaspati;
one desiring sensory power (*indriya*), Indra; one desiring progeny, the Prajāpatis; one desiring fortune (*śrī*), the Goddess Māyā; and one desiring splendor (*tejas*), the Fire-god (*vibhāvasu*).
One desiring wealth should worship the Vasus; one who is powerful and desires prowess, the Rudras;
one desiring food, Aditi; and one desiring heaven, the sons of Aditi. One desiring sovereignty should worship the Viśvedevas, and one who seeks to accomplish the goals of the people, the Sādhyas.
One desiring long life should worship the two Aśvin deities; one desiring prosperity should worship Ilā;
a person desiring stability should worship Rodasī, the mothers of the worlds; one desiring beauty should worship the Gandharvas; and one desiring a wife should worship the Apsaras Urvaśī.
One who desires sovereignty over all should worship Parameṣṭhin;
one who desires fame should perform the sacrifice to Yajña; one who desires a treasury should worship Pracetas;
one who desires knowledge should worship Giriśa; and one who desires a harmonious marriage should worship Umā Satī.
For the sake of dharma and artha, one should worship Uttamaśloka while extending the lineage;
one desiring protection should worship the Puṇyajanas; one desiring vigor should worship the hosts of Maruts;
one desiring sovereignty should worship the Manus and the gods; and one practicing malevolent magic should worship Nirṛti.
One who desires sense-objects should worship Soma; one who is free from desire should worship the Supreme Person.
Whether free from desire or desiring all things, a person of noble intellect who desires liberation should worship the Supreme Person with intense yoga of devotion.
For those who perform sacrifices in this world, the arising of the highest good is precisely this: an unwavering devotion to the Blessed Lord born from association with His devotees;
and that knowledge in which the wheel of the waves of the *guṇas* no longer turns back.
Wherein there is clarity of self and non-attachment to the modes of nature,
which is the path esteemed for liberation— indeed, the yoga of devotion—
who that is at peace would not take delight in the narrations of Hari?
Śaunaka said:
O bull of the Bharatas, having heard what was thus spoken,
what else did the king further question the sage Vyāsa, the seer and poet?
O learned Sūta, you ought to speak this for us who desire to hear it;
for the discourses of the virtuous in an assembly surely culminate in stories of Hari.
That king, the Pāṇḍava, was indeed a great chariot-warrior and a devotee of the Lord.
Playing with children's toys, he took up the pastimes of Kṛṣṇa; and the venerable son of Vyāsa as well was devoted solely to Vāsudeva,
for the virtues of the Wide-Strider are sublime when encountered in the assembly of the virtuous.
Rising and setting, this sun indeed steals away the lifespan of men;
yet that moment of his which has been spent in conversation concerning the One of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka) is truly gained.
Do not trees live? And do bellows not breathe?
Do other animals in the village not eat and not urinate? A man who is praised as being like a dog, a dog, a boar, a camel,
or a donkey is indeed an animal, for he has never once brought the name of the elder brother of Gadā (Baladeva) to his ears.
O Sūta, that man in whose ear-cavity the heroic strides of Urukrama have not entered,

and whose tongue, though virtuous, does not sing the songs of the Wide-Strider like a female frog; and whose head, though adorned with a silken crown, does not bow down to Mukunda— that head is nothing but a burden.

Those two hands of ours do not perform worship to Hari, nor do they possess shimmering golden bracelets; those two eyes of ours act like peacock feathers for men who do not gaze upon the emblems of Viṣṇu;
and those two feet of ours share the birth of trees, for they do not follow the sacred sites of Hari.
A mortal who does not ever obtain the dust from the feet of the devotees of the Lord is a mere corpse while living;

and that man who, though breathing, does not know the fragrance of the tulasi plant—the lotus-feet of Śrī Viṣṇu—is likewise a corpse. Alas, this heart is surely made of stone, since it is not moved even when the names of Hari are being grasped!

When there is no change, yet tears in the eyes and horripilation on the body hairs—then, my dear friend, speak what is agreeable to the mind; you speak like one who is foremost among the devotees of the Lord.
For this is exactly what the son of Vyāsa, the expert in the knowledge of the Self, said when he was properly questioned by the King.
Sūta said:
Having understood these words of the son of Vyāsa as the definitive certainty of truth regarding the Self,
the son of Uttara fixed his mind firmly upon Kṛṣṇa.
He abandoned the constant sense of "mineness" (mamatā) regarding his children, wife, sons, home, cattle, wealth, kinsmen, and even his unimpaired kingdom;
and it was concerning this very matter that he asked me, O best of beings, which you now ask of me.
Having heard of the power of Kṛṣṇa, he became full of faith; being high-minded, he understood the true nature of things, renounced the activities pertaining to the three goals of life,
and attained a firm state of self-identification with the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva.
The King said:
"O sinless Brahmin, your words are most appropriate for you who are all-knowing;
as you narrate the stories of Hari, my darkness is being shattered."
I desire to know further, O Blessed One, how by Your own *māyā* You create this universe, which is difficult even for the supreme lords to conceive;
and how the All-pervading One protects it, and how He withdraws it once again.

O Brahmin, whatever power the Supreme Person, the Lord of infinite power, relies upon to sport with Himself— playing, sporting, and transforming— it is surely the work of the Blessed Hari, whose deeds are marvelous.
The activity of even the sages appears difficult to comprehend, just as the Supreme Lord alone,
though one, manifests the qualities of *prakṛti* either simultaneously or sequentially,
performing manifold deeds through various births.
"I have this doubt; may the Blessed One explain it to me, for you are indeed well-versed in the Veda as expressed in words and in the Supreme Reality.
Sūta said:
Thus addressed by the king regarding the narration of the qualities of Hari,
he called to mind Hṛṣīkeśa and proceeded to reply.
Śrī Śuka said:

Obeisances to the Supreme Person, the most exalted, who by the play of creation, maintenance, and dissolution has assumed the three potencies; who dwells within all embodied beings, whose path is imperceptible, and who repeatedly cuts away the suffering of the virtuous while remaining impossible for the wicked to attain. Obeisances again to Him whose form is composed of the totality of all existence.

Salutations again to You who grant Your grace even to those established in the stage of the paramahaṃsas; salutations, salutations to You, the bull among the Sātvatas, who are the farthest limit for even the most persistent practitioners of yoga. Salutations to You who shall delight in Your own abode, the Brahman, through a glory that has cast aside all equality and superiority.

Salutations again and again to Him of auspicious fame, whose glorification, remembrance, sight, salutation, hearing, and worship instantly shake off the impurities of the world. For by approaching His feet, the wise cast away attachment to both [the internal and external] through the inner self.
For those who have reached Him find the goal of Brahman with their weariness dispelled; salutations again and again to that Subhadraśravas.

Ascetics, those devoted to charity, the illustrious, the wise, the knowers of mantras, and the most auspicious—without surrendering to Him, they do not find security; salutations again and again to that Subhadraśravas.

Salutations to that Sovereign Lord, by taking refuge in whom the Kirātas, Hūṇas, Āndhras, Pulindas, Pulkasas, Ābhīras, Śumbhas, Yavanas, Khasas, and others— whatever sinners there may be— are purified. He is this very Self of those who possess self-mastery, consisting of the three Vedas, consisting of dharma, and consisting of austerity.
May the Lord, whose true nature was deliberated upon by Brahmā, Śiva, and others who had cast aside all deceit, be gracious.

May the Blessed One—the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Lord of Creatures, the Lord of Intelligence, the Lord of the Worlds, the Lord of the Earth, and the refuge and master of the Andhakas, Vṛṣṇis, and Sātvatas; may the Blessed One, the Lord of the virtuous, be gracious unto me.

When they behold the reality of the Self with an intellect purified by meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon contemplation of His feet, the sages speak of this according to their own inclination; may that Lord Mukunda be gracious unto me.
By whom, in the past, the river Sarasvatī was impelled within the heart of the Unborn One, expanding His true remembrance.

May that Bull among sages, who is said to have manifested from this [Veda] characterized by its own specific marks, be gracious toward me. May the Blessed One, who is the sixteenfold Self, who having fashioned these cities with the great elements lies within them as the Puruṣa, and who enjoys the sixteen qualities therein, adorn my words.
"Obeisance to that Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the Creator,
from whose gentle lotus-face the smile that purifies knowledge flows forth.
O King, it was this very [knowledge] that the Self-born (Brahmā) imparted to Nārada when he questioned him."
Vedagarbha spoke that which Hari himself had declared regarding his own nature.
Nārada said:
"O God of gods, obeisance be unto you, O creator of beings, O first-born!"

Know that knowledge which reveals the true nature of the Self; O Lord, tell me in truth that reality— its form, its foundation, from whence this world was created, wherein it is established, what is supreme, and what it truly is.
For you know all this, O Lord of the past, the future, and the present;
the entire universe is as clearly perceived by your supreme knowledge as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of your hand.
You are that which possesses knowledge, that upon which it rests, that which is beyond it, and that whose very nature it is.
Alone, You create all beings by means of Your own power of illusion (*māyā*) through those very beings; O Self, You sustain them without Yourself being overcome by destruction,
having taken hold of Your own power, like a tireless spider.
O All-pervading Lord, I do not know what is superior to You, nor what is inferior, nor what is equal;

there exists nothing else besides You that can be conceived through name, form, or quality, whether it be existent or non-existent. Yet, you, being perfectly composed, performed formidable austerities.
Therefore, you weary me and cast suspicion upon others.
O omniscient Lord of all, please explain all this to me as I ask it,
so that I may understand it as instructed by You.
Brahmā said:
"O child, this inquiry of yours is perfectly suited to one who is compassionate;
for you have urged me, O gentle one, to reveal the prowess of the Blessed Lord."
"O sir, that which you tell me is not false;
for you do not know that which is beyond me,
since it is by my own light that the universe is illumined, and I am the one who illumines it."
Just as the sun, fire, the moon, and the constellations, planets, and stars [shine],
let us meditate upon that Blessed Lord Vāsudeva,
by whose invincible *māyā* they call me the Teacher of the World.
Those of perverted intellect, deluded by Him, boast "I" and "mine," even though they are ashamed to stand within the range of His vision.
[He is] matter, action, time, nature, and indeed the individual soul.
O Brahmin, in reality there is no other entity whatsoever that is superior to Vāsudeva. The Vedas have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal; the gods are born from the limbs of Nārāyaṇa;
the worlds have Nārāyaṇa as their ultimate support; and sacrifices have Nārāyaṇa as their final aim.
Yoga is centered on Nārāyaṇa; austerity is centered on Nārāyaṇa;
knowledge is centered on Nārāyaṇa; and the ultimate goal is centered on Nārāyaṇa—even for that Lord who is the seer, the immutable, and the Self of all.
"I create that which is to be created; though I am uncreated, I am impelled by His mere glance.

Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these are the three qualities of the one who is beyond qualities (nirguṇa). They are assumed by the pervasive Lord through Māyā for the purposes of maintenance, creation, and dissolution."

The modes of nature (*guṇas*), which serve as the substrata for substance, knowledge, and action, and for the states of being the effect, the cause, and the agent, perpetually bind the illusory person (*māyin*) who is eternally free.
This very Lord, Adhokṣaja, is endowed with these three marks.
O Brahmin, the Lord, who is the master of all and of me as well, whose movement is perfectly characterized,
desiring to manifest Himself through His own power of illusion (*māyā*), took up time, action, and inherent nature—
whatever was obtained by His own will— in order to become manifold.
From time arises the transformation of the qualities (*guṇa*), which is evolution by its own nature;
from the Great One (*mahat*), presided over by the Puruṣa, birth proceeds through the activity of karma.
And from the Great One undergoing transformation, augmented by *rajas* and *sattva*, [the ego-sense arises].
But that which was dominated by *tamas*, consisting of the nature of substance, knowledge, and action, is called *ahaṃkāra*; undergoing transformation, it became threefold through its divisions:
the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *tāmasa*.
O Lord, there are the power of matter (*dravya-śakti*), the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).

From the *bhūtādi* element, which is characterized by *tamas*, undergoing transformation, space (*nabhas*) arose. Its subtle constituent (*mātrā*) is the quality of sound (*śabda*), which serves as the link between the seer and the seen.
Then, from the transformation of ether, there arose the wind, which has touch as its quality;
through the succession of the supreme, it possesses sound as well, and is the vital breath, vigor, endurance, and strength.
Furthermore, from the transformation of the wind, by virtue of time, action, and inherent nature—
From that, fire indeed arose, possessing form, touch, and sound.
From fire, as it underwent transformation, water was produced, consisting of taste;
and water, by following the sequence of the supreme, came to possess form, touch, and sound.
But from the water undergoing transformation, there arose the specific quality of smell;
through the sequence of the subsequent elements, it became endowed with the qualities of taste, touch, sound, and form.
From the *vaikārika* [ego], the mind was born, as were the ten *vaikārika* gods.

From the Taijasa ego, as it underwent transformation, there arose the ten sense organs: the quarters, wind, sun, Varuṇa, the Aśvins, fire, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, and Kāla. Furthermore, the power of cognition and the power of action—the intellect and the vital breath—also emerged from the Taijasa.
Ear, skin, nose, eyes, tongue, speech, hands, genitals, feet,

and anus— O best of the knowers of Brahman, when these entities, which are the elements, the senses, the mind, and the qualities, were unable to effect the construction of their own abodes because they were unattached, [then the Lord entered them].
Then, impelled by the power of the Lord, they united with one another and,
taking recourse to both the existent and the non-existent, created this universe;
for at the end of many thousands of cycles of years, that egg was resting upon the waters.
Abiding in time, karma, and inherent nature, the Jīva brought the non-living to life.
That very Puruṣa, having emerged from the split egg,
possessed a thousand thighs, feet, arms, and eyes, and a thousand faces and heads.
The wise conceive of the worlds as being formed from the limbs of this [Puruṣa]:
the seven lower worlds from his hips and so forth, and the seven upper worlds from his loins and so forth.
Of this Puruṣa, the mouth is Brahman and the arms are Kṣatra.
From the thighs of the Blessed One was born the Vaiśya, and from His feet the Śūdra. The world of Bhūr was fashioned from His feet, and Bhuvarloka from His navel.
Svarloka arose from the heart of the Great-Souled One, and Maharloka from His chest.
Janaloka is situated in His neck, and Tapoloka arises from His two breasts;
Satyaloka, the eternal realm of Brahmā, is formed from His heads. From the waist of the All-pervading Lord, Atala is fashioned, and Vitala from His thighs.
With his knees he is Śuddha, with his shanks Sutala, with his ankles Mahātala, with the foreparts of his feet Rasātala,
and with the soles of his feet Pātāla; thus the Person consists of the worlds.

"The realm of the earth (bhūrloka) was fashioned from his feet, the realm of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka) from his navel, and the heavenly realm (svarloka) from his head— such is the conception of the worlds. Thus spoke Brahmā.
The mouth is the field for speech and fire; the seven constituent elements are the field for the Vedic meters;

the tongue is the field for oblations to the gods, offerings to the ancestors, nectar, and food, as well as for all tastes; and the two nostrils are the supreme abode for all vital breaths and the wind.
The nose belongs to the Aśvins and the medicinal herbs; the eyes belong to Modā and Pramodā, to forms, to splendors, to the heavens, and to the sun;
the ears belong to the quarters of space and the sacred fords; and the sense of hearing belongs to space and sound.
His body is the vessel for the essence of all things and for good fortune;
his skin is indeed that of the wind of touch and of the universal sacrifice; and his body hairs are of the nature of plants, by which the sacrifice is fully provided.
His hair, beard, and nails are those of stones, iron, clouds, and lightning;
his arms are those of the world-protectors who generally perform the work of preservation;
and his prowess is that of the realms of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar, as well as of security and refuge.
The feet of Hari, the bestower of all desired boons, are the seat of the waters; the generative organ is that of Parjanya, the lord of progeny,
for the sake of procreation and the bliss of sexual pleasure.
O Nārada, the anus is said to belong to Yama, Mitra, Parimokṣa,
Hiṃsā, Nirṛti, Mṛtyu, and Niraya; the posterior opening belongs to Parābhūti, Adharma, and Tamas.
The channels of the rivers and streams are his veins; the collection of bones is the mountains;
the unmanifest oceans of fluids are his belly; and the heart is known as the seat of the mind and the place of dissolution for all beings.
I am the supreme Self and the ultimate refuge of Dharma, of you, of me, of the Kumāras, and of Bhava; likewise of consciousness, of the individual soul, and of the Supreme Being.
I, you, Bhava, and these sages born before us are all one.
Gods, demons, humans, serpents, birds, beasts, and reptiles;
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Yakṣas, hosts of Rākṣasas, spirits, and Uragas;
cattle, ancestors, Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Cāraṇas, and trees—[all these were present].
And other various living beings— those dwelling in water, on land, and in the sky; the planets, constellations, comets, stars, lightning, and thunderclouds—
all this, whatever has been, whatever will be, and whatever is now, is indeed the Puruṣa alone.
By him this entire universe is pervaded, and he stands as the span of a cubit; heating his own abode, this vital breath heats the exterior as well.
Thus, heating the Virāj, the Supreme Person heats both the interior and the exterior.

He is the Lord of immortality and fearlessness; because He has transcended mortal food, O Brahmin, this majesty of the Puruṣa is difficult to surpass. Those who know the state of the Person's abiding recognize all beings as being in His feet.
Immortality, security, and fearlessness were established upon the heads of the three-headed one;
his other three feet were outside the triple-world, consisting of those stages of life (āśramas) belonging to those who do not procreate,
while the householder’s stage, which does not involve great vows, remained within the triple-world.
He traversed both paths—the one of eating and the one of not eating—which are both ignorance and knowledge; the Person, however, is the support of both.
From Him was born the cosmic egg, the Virāṭ, consisting of the elements, the senses, and the qualities.
That substance pervaded the entire universe, heating it with its rays like the sun;
when I was born from the lotus-navel of that Great Soul,
I did not know the materials for sacrifice apart from the limbs of the Puruṣa.
Among those [requirements for sacrifice] were the sacrificial animals, the *savanaspatis*, and the *kuśa* grass;
this very place of divine worship (*devayajana*), and time endowed with excellent qualities;
as well as the materials: herbs, fats, liquids, metals, earth, and water.
O best of beings, the *Ṛg-veda*, *Yajur-veda*, and *Sāma-veda*; the fourfold sacrificial office (*cāturhotra*);
the names, the mantras, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and the vows; the sequence of deities, the ritual manual (*kalpa*), the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), and the tantric system itself.
"Destinies and thoughts, as well as atonement and surrender—
these materials have been gathered by me from the limbs of the Supreme Person.
Thus, I am one who has gathered these materials from the limbs of the Supreme Person.
With that very sacrifice, they worshipped that same Lord, the Puruṣa.
Then these nine brothers of theirs, the lords of progeny,
being well-composed, worshipped the manifest and unmanifest Puruṣa.
Then, in due course, the Manus, other sages,
the ancestors, the gods, the Daityas, and human beings worshipped the All-pervading Lord with sacrifices; for this entire universe is established within the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa.
At the beginning of creation, I—though inherently devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)—assume the quality of *rajas* through His power;
directed by Him, I create, and Hara destroys under His control. Upholding the three energies (*tri-śakti*), He protects the universe in the form of Puruṣa.
"Thus has this been told to you, my dear, just as you have inquired;
there is nothing else, whether existent or non-existent in nature, that can be produced apart from the Blessed Lord.
My speech, O dear one, is never observed to be false, nor indeed does my mind ever turn toward what is untrue."
My senses do not fall upon the path of the unreal, for Hari has been held within my heart by my yearning.

Being composed through that skillful yoga, I— who am composed of the Vedas and composed of austerity, and who am the Lord of the Prajāpatis honored by them— did not perceive Him from whom I myself have sprung.
I bow to His feet, which grant auspiciousness and are the destroyers of worldly existence for those who have approached them;
for He has fully pervaded the manifestation of His own *māyā* as the sky pervades space—how then could others reach His inner self?
Neither I, nor you, nor Vāmadeva knows the true course of that Reality, much less other gods.
Those whose intellects are deluded by His māyā perceive this created world as being equal to themselves; yet we, like ourselves, sing of the deeds of His incarnations—
homage to that Blessed One whom they do not know in truth.

This very same primordial Person, unborn, creates himself from himself by means of himself in every kalpa; he restrains himself and protects himself. His knowledge is pure, absolute, inward-turned, and perfectly established.
O Sage, when that very Reality— which is truth, full, without beginning or end, devoid of qualities, eternal, and non-dual—
is perceived by sages whose minds, senses, and inner dispositions are perfectly tranquil; yet,
when it is obscured and distorted by fallacious arguments, [it is no longer seen].
The first incarnation of the Supreme Person is Time, inherent nature, the existent and non-existent, and the mind;
He is the substance, the transformation, the qualities, the senses, the cosmic egg (Virāṭ), the self-ruler (Svarāṭ), the stationary, and the moving—all these belong to the Infinite One.
I, Śiva, and these lords of creatures such as Dakṣa and yourself are also His manifestations.
The guardians of the heavenly world, the guardians of the world of birds, the guardians of the world of men, and the guardians of the netherworld;
the lords of the Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and Cāraṇas; those who are the masters of the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Uragas, and Nāgas;
and those who are the preeminent sages among Ṛṣis, the lords of the Pitṛs, the sovereigns of the Daityas, Siddhas, and Dānavas.
And others—those who are lords of the pretas, piśācas, bhūtas, kūṣmāṇḍas, yātudhānas, beasts, and birds;
and whatever else in the world, O Blessed One, is possessed of majesty, vigor, power, and forbearance;
that which is an ocean of splendor, modesty, prosperity, and self-possession, and which is wondrous in its nature—whether it be a supreme reality or a formless entity possessing form.

I shall describe in due order these beautiful pastimes of the Infinite Person, which the sages declare to be His primary incarnations, so that by drinking them in, the impurities of the ears may be dried up.
Brahmā said:
Therein, Ananta, assuming the form of a boar consisting of all sacrifices, raised his snout to lift up the surface of the earth;
and within the great ocean, he encountered the primordial Daitya who had approached him.
Like the wielder of the thunderbolt tearing apart a mountain with his tusk, he tore him asunder.
Suyajña, born of Ruci, begot the Suyamas;
and the son of Ākūti begot the immortals through Dakṣiṇā.
Because he removed the great suffering of the three worlds,
he was called "Hari" by Svāyambhuva Manu; and,
O twice-born one, he was born in the house of Kardama from Devahūtī.

Together with his nine wives, he spoke of his own spiritual state to his mother; having shaken off the impurity of his own nature— the mire of attachment to the material qualities— he attained the destination of Kapila.
To Atri, who longed for offspring, the Blessed One, being pleased, said, "I myself am given by me"; thus he is Datta. Those whose bodies have been purified by the dust of his lotus feet—
The Yadus, Haihayas, and others attained both kinds of yogic power;
for in the beginning, through my penance performed with the desire to create various worlds, he who was originally Sanāt became the possessor of the four powers (Catussan).
O sages, you have correctly declared the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) as it was perceived by Him within Himself, which had been destroyed here at the dissolution of the previous kalpa;
[that Self] was born in the form of Dharma’s offspring from the daughter of Dakṣa.
Nārāyaṇa and Nara, by the power of their own austerity,
having perceived that the Lord’s observance of his vows was being violated,
were unable for the goddesses— the armies of the bodiless god of love— to effect a union with him.
Surely the wise burn away desire with a glance of wrath; yet do they not burn that unbearable wrath which burns them? For this very wrath fears to enter into the interval between them.
"How indeed could desire ever again take refuge in his mind— he who,
though but a child, has gone to the forests for asceticism after being pierced by the feathered arrows discharged by his co-wife in the presence of the king?"
Being pleased with him who praised Him, He granted him the eternal state;
the divine sages praise that which is above and below.
When he had gone astray, the thunderbolt of the twice-born’s words [struck] him.
Having been entreated by him who was falling into hell with his human merit exhausted, he saved him and obtained the status of a son in this world; by him,
all the treasures of the earth were milked.
From Nābhi was born this bull among men, the son of Sudevi, who, possessing equal vision toward all, practiced the yoga-conduct of the dull-witted,
which the seers declare to be the state of the Paramahaṃsas.
At that sacrificial session,
the Blessed Lord Hayaśīrṣa himself— the Person of Sacrifice (Yajñapuruṣa), golden-hued— was present, composed in mind, with his senses tranquil, and entirely free from attachment.
Consisting of the Vedic meters, consisting of sacrifice, and being the self of all deities,
from his nostrils as he breathed forth, there arose the hundredfold words of the Vedas;
and at the time of the end of the age, he was perceived by Manu in the form of a fish.
Consisting of earth, the refuge for all classes of living beings,
he took up my faces that had been submerged in the waters of great fear and sported there according to the paths of the Vedas.
In the Ocean of Milk, while the leaders of the hosts of gods and demons were churning it for the sake of obtaining the nectar of immortality, the Primal God,
assuming the form of a tortoise, supported the mountain on his back.

With a moment's sleep, he caused the mountain to roll; with the itching of his mane, he destroyed the great fear of the inhabitants of the triple heaven. Assuming the form of Nṛsiṃha, his face became terrifying with its furrowed brows and bared fangs.
As the lord of the Daityas rushed forward with his mace, [the Lord] quickly struck him down upon his own thigh from nearby and tore the quivering demon apart with his claws; meanwhile,
within the lake, [the demon] was seized by the foot by one of immense strength.
Seized by the crocodile, the lord of the herd, his hands like lotuses, being distressed, said this:
"O Primordial Being, Lord of all the worlds,
whose sacred fame is auspicious to hear and whose very name is a blessing!"
Having heard that he was seeking his wife, the immeasurable Hari,
whose weapon is the discus, mounted upon the king of birds and,
with his discus, tore open the mouth of the crocodile from which [he had rescued her].
Taking him by the hand, the Blessed One compassionately lifted him up;
though he was the youngest among the sons of Aditi, he was superior to them in virtues,
for as the presiding deity of sacrifice, he traversed these worlds.
He seized the earth by means of the Vāmana incarnation under the pretext of three paces;

yet, while traveling on the path, he was not moved from his purpose by the lords, for he required nothing other than a request. This is not the wealth of Bali; rather, it is the purification of the feet of the Wide-striding Lord.
The waters attained the sovereignty of the gods because he,
having promised something, did not wish to do anything else than that;
O dear one, he mentally offered himself to Hari.
And to you, O Nārada, the Lord, being greatly pleased by your profound devotion, spoke of yoga and the Bhāgavata knowledge, which is a lamp illuminating the true nature of the Self.
Moreover, those who take refuge in Vāsudeva immediately attain [liberation]; and he,
the sustainer of the lineage of Manu, bears his own unimpeded discus and splendor throughout the ten directions during the various Manvantaras.
Among wicked kings, he established punishment; and by his deeds, he spread his own beloved fame among the truthful people as Tripṛṣṭha.
And the Blessed One himself became Dhanvantari, the very embodiment of glory.
By its very name, it swiftly destroys the many ailments of men; in sacrifice, it secures a share [for the sacrificer] and bestows immortal life;
having descended into the world, it instructs them in the science of longevity.

That high-souled one of fierce valor, who desires to uproot the thorn of the earth— the Kṣatriya who, having abandoned the path and become a slayer of Brahmins, was brought forth by ritual decree for his own destruction and seeks only the sufferings of hell— uproots him indeed.
Having descended twenty-one times into the lineage of Ikṣvāku by the command of his guru, you, O Lord of Kalās, with your face made gracious by our favor, [acted] with your broad-edged axe.

Standing there with his beloved wife and younger brother, he entered the forest in which the ten-headed Rāvaṇa, having provoked him to enmity, met with calamity; it was from him that the ocean, its limbs trembling with rising fear, offered [the jewel].
Desiring to burn the city of his enemy instantly like Śiva,
he heated the path with his gaze, blood-red with rage stirred by his friend, which filled the circle of sea-monsters, serpents, and crocodiles from afar.
With his teeth, he will mock the elephants of the world-dwellers as they are crushed by the touch of his chest; laughing aloud,
he will instantly carry away the life-breaths of the abductor of his wife.
With the twanging of his bow resounding over the army, he—
whose hair was white and black— manifested as a partial incarnation for the sake of relieving the suffering of the earth, which had been crushed by the hosts of the enemies of the gods.
Once born, he will perform deeds that reveal his path to the people,
deeds which are bound up with his own greatness—
such as the taking of life from a female owl by means of a mere infant.
And by the footstep of the Three-Monthed One, a cart was overturned;
otherwise, the uprooting of those two sky-touching trees by Arjuna would not have been possible.

Indeed, that [serpent] which had made the cattle of Vraja drink poisoned water, and which the cowherds had revived with a rain of their glance of grace— that [serpent], whose tongue was agitated by the potency of extreme poison, [was killed] for the sake of purification.

While wandering by the river, he would drive away venomous snakes; yet that same deed seemed divine when, lying down at night while the pure forest was being consumed by a forest fire, he remained unharmed.
"Closing their eyes, he, together with his army and possessing unattainable prowess, will lead away Vraja from here before its time has ended; therefore,
seize whatever belongings his mother may have."
The cord of the son did not measure that [universe] of his;
for when Gopī beheld the worlds within the mouth of Him as He yawned, her mind became filled with apprehension, and she was awakened.
And he will deliver Nanda from the fear of Varuṇa’s noose,
as well as the cowherds who were hidden in caves by the son of Maya,
and those who were occupied during the day and sleeping at night from extreme exhaustion.
When the sacrifice was obstructed by the cowherds and the rain-god poured down rain upon Vraja, he, desiring to protect the cattle out of compassion, led Gokula to the world of Vaikuṇṭha.

For seven days, he sported effortlessly with his single, faultless hand upon the mountain, supporting it like a mushroom-stalk during a great rain; while playing in the forest at night, which was as white as the rays of the moon.
Intent on the *rāsa* dance, with his voice made resonant by long,
melodious notes, Hari will sever the head of the follower of Kubera who steals away the hearts of the women of Vraja, whose passion is inflamed by his song.
And those such as Pralamba, Khara, Dardura, Keśī, Ariṣṭa, Malla, Ibhaka, Kaṃsa, the Yavana, Kapī, Pauṇḍraka,
and others, as well as Śālva, Kuja, Balvala, and Dantavakra—
Sapta, Ukṣa, Śambara, Vidūratha, Rukmin, and other leaders;
those who were skilled in assembly and took up their bows in battle—
the Kāmbojas, Matsyas, Kurus, Sṛñjayas, Kaikayas, and others.
O Balarāma, Arjuna, and Bhīma, they will vanish from sight;
by means of Hari appearing under a deceptive guise, he will lead them to his own abode,
having observed those whose intellects have been clouded by time.
Alas, for those of short lifespan, the Veda— whose further shore is so distant—
is revealed age after age by you, born of Satyavatī;
for you shall divide that tree of the Vedas branch by branch.
To those enemies of the gods who were established on the path of the Vedas, he [Hiraṇyakaśipu] granted cities constructed by Maya that were invisible to the eyes,
as well as the delusion of intellect and excessive sensual allurements for those who were destroying the worlds.

When even in the dwellings of the virtuous there are no discourses on Hari, those twice-born men who adopt various guises and speak much that is contrary to dharma become heretics; they are outcasts among men and serve as gods for the common folk.
Where there will be no words such as "svāhā," "svadhā," or "vaṣaṭ," the Blessed One will become the teacher at the end of the Kali age; [in the previous] creation,
I was the penance and the nine sages who were the lords of progeny.
Then, in due course, the gods and lords of the earth performed sacrifices for dharma;
but in the end, the asuras and others, under the sway of anger and driven by unrighteousness,
became these manifestations of Māyā, possessing great power.
Who here is capable of enumerating the heroic powers of Viṣṇu? He who, as a seer, measured even the earthly particles of dust; he who, with his unswerving stride, propped up the triple-heavened sky.
Since I do not know the end of that Great Compassionate One who dwells in the equilibrium of the three qualities, nor do these sages born before me;
how then could those who are inferior know it?
Even now, Śeṣa— the primordial deity with a thousand faces— remains unable to reach the end of his qualities while singing them;
may that very Lord Ananta show compassion toward those [who seek him].
If they have taken refuge in the feet of the Soul of All with complete sincerity,
they cross over the insurmountable divine illusion; for them,
there is no thought of "mine" or "I" regarding that which is to be devoured by dogs and jackals.
"O dear one, I indeed know the supreme power of yoga-māyā; so do you, Lord Śiva, the chief of the Daityas,
the wife of Manu, Manu himself, and his sons."
Prācīnabarhis, Ṛbhu, Aṅga, and Dhruva; Ikṣvāku, Rila, Mucukunda, Videha,
Gādhi, Raghu, Ambarīṣa, Sagara, Gaya, Nahuṣa, and others.
Māndhātṛ, Alarka, Śatadhanvan, Anarantideva, Devavrata, Bali, Amūrtarayas, Dilīpa,
Saubhari, Uttaṅka, Śibi, Devala, and Pippalāda.
Sārasvata, Uddhava, Parāśara, and Bhūriṣeṇa;
and others such as Vibhīṣaṇa, Hanūmat, Upendradatta,
Pārtha, Arṣṭiṣeṇa, Vidura, and the eminent Śrutadeva.
Indeed,
even women, Śūdras, Hūṇas, Śabaras, and those of sinful livelihood,
come to know and transcend the divine illusion (devamāyā) if they are devoted to the wonderful sequence [of the Lord's deeds] and possess disciplined character and training.
What need is there to mention those who possess the learning and retention of the Vedas? Even animals [aspire to] that reality of the Supreme Self, which is eternally peaceful, fearless,
pure consciousness alone, stainless, equal, and beyond both being and non-being.

That place of the Supreme Person, the Blessed One, is where sound— which possesses many causal agents for the purpose of action— does not exist, and where Māyā retreats in shame when she comes face to face with Him.

That which the knowers call Brahman— the imperishable bliss free from sorrow— is that toward which ascetics, having restrained their senses, direct themselves and abandon the weapon of Yama, just as Indra, the self-ruling lord, abandons the shovel used for digging a water-pit.
He is the Lord, the sovereign even over all that is auspicious, from whom proceeds the manifestation of this being— though it is ordained by the very nature of its own existence—
even as the body dissolves when its constituent elements depart.
Just as the sky is not shattered there, so the Person (puruṣa) is not destroyed; he is the self-effulgent one.
This very Lord, the creator of the universe, has been described to you in brief, O dear one—Hari, who is none other than that from which both the existent and the non-existent proceed.

"This work called *Bhāgavata*, which was spoken by the Blessed One to me— this is a compendium of His manifestations; you should expand it so that devotion toward the Blessed Lord Hari may arise in men."
Having resolved, "He is the Self of all, the support of everything," one who describes His illusory power (*māyā*), approves of that Lord as He describes it,
and constantly hears of it with faith, is not deluded by *māyā* regarding the Self.
The King said:
O Brahmin, as urged by Brahmā, you have described the qualities of the One who is beyond all qualities;
tell me how Nārada, who has the vision of the gods, spoke to each person according to their need.

O best among those who know the truth, I desire to know this reality: the stories of Hari, whose prowess is wondrous, which bring auspiciousness to the world. O illustrious one, relate them to me, for I am devoted to the Self of all.
Having fixed my mind without attachment upon Kṛṣṇa, I shall cast off this body while constantly listening with faith and chanting of his own deeds;
before long, the Blessed One will enter my heart.
Having entered the lotus-heart of his own people through the aperture of the ear,
Kṛṣṇa shakes off their impurity just as autumn does that of water. A person whose self has been thus cleansed does not abandon the root of Kṛṣṇa’s feet.
Like a traveler who has cast off all afflictions and reached his own refuge;
O Brahman, as you understand how this body is composed of elements, whether its commencement through those elements occurs by chance or by some cause.
From whose belly there arose a lotus, the characteristic abode of the worlds; indeed,
as vast as this Puruṣa is with his various limbs,
so vast is he said to be, appearing as if possessed of structural limbs.

The Unborn One, the soul of all beings, creates all creatures by whose grace the one born from the navel-lotus beheld that form; and he, moreover, is the Person in whom the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe reside.
Having withdrawn his own *māyā*, the Lord of *māyā*, who dwells in the secret cave of all beings, lies down;
we have heard that the worlds together with their guardians were fashioned in the past from the limbs of the Supreme Person (*puruṣa*),
and that the limbs of this [Person] are the worlds together with their guardians.
Whatever constitutes a kalpa or a vikalpa, and however time is inferred; whatever is expressed by the terms "past," "future," and "present," and whatever measure of lifespan belongs to the existent;
and whatever subtle or gross continuity of time is observed—[all these are but its manifestations].

O best of the twice-born, as many as are the courses of karma and of what nature they are; in which [course] the accumulation of karma occurs, and how and by whom it is grasped; and the transformation of the qualities (*guṇa*) and those possessing qualities who desire such change—[all this has been told].
The origin of the earth, the netherworlds, the quarters, the sky, the planets, the constellations,
and the mountains; as well as the origin of the rivers, oceans, islands, and the inhabitants of these worlds—
the measurement of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍakośa*) is thus described according to its internal and external divisions.
The life of the great ones, the determination of the social classes and stages of life, the ages (yugas) and the measurement of the ages, the dharma that prevails in each age,
and the most wonderful accounts of the incarnations of Hari.
The common duty of human beings and their specific duties as they are;
the duty of guilds and of royal sages living in times of distress;
the enumeration of the principles, their definitions, and the characteristics of their causes.
The method for propitiating the Supreme Person, the practice of spiritual yoga,
the attainment of the sovereignty of the Lords of Yoga, the dissolution of the subtle body for yogis,
and the contents of the Vedas, Upavedas, Dharmashastras, Itihasas, and Puranas— [all these were revealed].
The dissolution of all beings, their manifestation, and their reabsorption;
the ordinances for sacrifices, charitable works, rites for desired ends, and the three goals of life;
the creation of those who follow after death, and the origin of heresy.
The bondage and liberation of the self, as well as its establishment in its own essential nature, [are explained];
how the Lord, independent of others, sports by means of His own *māyā*,
or how, having withdrawn that *māyā*, the omnipresent Lord remains indifferent like a witness.
O Blessed One, O Great Sage, you ought to explain all of this in its true essence and in due order to me, who have sought refuge; for in this matter,
you are indeed the authority, just as Parameṣṭhin is to the Self-born Brahmā.
Others, moreover, follow what was performed by their ancestors in former times.
O Brahmin, my vital breaths do not depart because of this fasting,
as I drink the nectar of immortality flowing from the ocean of his words.
Sūta said:
Thus invited by the king to discourse upon the Lord of the virtuous,
the son of Brahmā, being greatly delighted, spoke in the assembly before Viṣṇurāta.
He spoke the Purāṇa named Bhāgavata, which is equal to the Veda,
as it had been proclaimed by the Blessed Lord to Brahmā when the Brahmakalpa had arrived—
whatever Parīkṣit, the bull among the Pāṇḍavas, inquired about.
He began to relate all of that in due order.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, apart from His own creative power (*māyā*), there is no other means for the perception of the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure consciousness.
A connection with objects does not truly apply to Him, just as it does not to the dreamer;
by means of His manifold illusory power, He appears in many forms, and while sporting among the modes of nature, He thinks "this is mine" and "I am this."

When, having transcended delusion, one rejoices in one's own supreme majesty which is beyond both time and *māyā*, and remains indifferent, having abandoned both— then that is the truth (*ṛta*) which the Blessed Lord spoke for the sake of purifying the reality of the self.
Showing his form to Brahmā, he who is devoted to unswerving vows—
that primordial god, the supreme teacher of the worlds— established himself upon his own throne and, desiring to create, gazed [upon the universe].
He did not find therein a vision that was approved for the procedure of creating the phenomenal world.

While reflecting thus, the omnipresent Lord once heard two syllables uttered twice within the waters—the sixteenth among the consonants (*sparśas*) and the twenty-first, which those who possess nothing know to be their wealth, O King.
Having heard them, and desiring to see their speaker, he looked in all directions; but seeing no one else there, he remained gazing.
Having occupied his own seat and reflected upon what was beneficial for him, he fixed his mind as if instructed in austerity.
For a thousand divine years, with unfailing vision, having conquered the vital breath and subdued both sets of senses,
that most excellent ascetic, composed in meditation, performed a penance that scorched all the worlds.

The Blessed Lord, having been honored by him, showed him his own supreme abode, which is beyond even the highest, free from affliction, delusion, and fear, and praised by those who have seen the Supreme Person; there,
rajas, tamas, and even sattva mixed with them do not prevail, nor does the onset of time.

There, Māyā has no power, much less those others who are devoted to Hari; there dwell the gods and asuras who worship Him—dark-complexioned and fair-skinned, lotus-eyed, clad in saffron robes, radiant, and well-formed;
all four-armed, adorned with excellent jewel-encrusted necklaces and ornaments, and possessed of great splendor.
Having the luster of coral, lapis lazuli, and lotus stalks, and adorned with shimmering earrings, crowns, and garlands,
he shines brilliantly on all sides surrounded by the radiant rows of celestial chariots belonging to the great-souled ones;
he gleams like the sky filled with banks of lightning-charged clouds, illuminated by the splendor of the most excellent women.

There, Śrī, in embodied form, pays homage in many ways with her divine manifestations at the feet of the Wide-Strider (Viṣṇu). Seated upon a swing and celebrated by the followers of Kusumāyudha (the God of Love), she sings of the deeds of her beloved.
There he beheld the Lord of all the Sātvatas, the Lord of Śrī, the Lord of sacrifice, and the Lord of the universe.
He saw the Lord attended by his foremost attendants, such as Sunanda, Nanda, Prabala, and Arhaṇa;
He was intent on showing favor to His servants, the nectar of whose eyes was His own form; His face and reddish eyes were brightened by a gracious smile;
He wore a crown and earrings, possessed four arms, was clad in yellow silk, and the Goddess Śrī was marked upon His chest.

He saw the Supreme Lord seated upon a most worthy throne, surrounded by His own four, sixteen, and five energies, endowed with His own eternal perfections as opposed to those found elsewhere which are transient; the Lord who delights in His own abode.
With his inner self overflowing with the joy of that vision, his body thrilled, and his eyes filled with tears from the weight of love, [he gazed upon Him].

He bowed at the lotus feet of Him who is reached by the path of the highest ascetics (*pāramahaṃsya*). To that wise one who had approached him with affection— worthy of his own command for the creation of progeny—
the beloved Lord, his mind filled with joy, spoke these words with a voice radiant with a gentle smile, while touching him with his hand.
The Blessed Lord said:

O Vedagarbha, I have been perfectly gratified by you through your long-sustained austerity, performed with the desire to create; for I am difficult to satisfy even by those who practice deceptive yoga.

"Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—from me, the Lord of boons, whatever you desire. O Brahmin, for men, the exertion toward the highest good culminates in the sight of Me. This vision of My world is the very manifestation of one's heart's desire."
Having heard this, you performed supreme austerity in secret;
yet, while you were deluded by karma, it was rejected by me there.
O sinless one, my austerity is my very heart, for I am the self of austerity itself.
"I create this universe by means of austerity alone; again, I swallow it by means of austerity;
I sustain the entire world by means of austerity; my virility is austerity, which is difficult to practice.
Brahmā said:

O Blessed One, as the presiding overseer of all beings, You indeed know with unobstructed wisdom what is intended within the heart; nevertheless, O Lord, grant the protection sought by me who am seeking Your protection.
May I know Your higher and lower forms, even though You Yourself are formless; for by the application of Your own *māyā*, You expand Yourself through various powers,
withdrawing, emitting, grasping, and sustaining Yourself by Yourself.

O Madhava, whose resolve is unfailing, just as a spider weaves its web, so please bestow upon me the wisdom directed toward that [Yourself]. I shall indeed perform what has been taught by Your Lordship without sloth.

O Lord, desiring the creation of progeny, I would have been bound had it not been for Your grace; therefore, as long as I am employed by You like a friend by a friend, I shall divide the people for the sake of the emission of creatures.
May I remain steadfast in Your service without confusion, and may I never be one whose pride is swollen with arrogance.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Accept this most secret knowledge of Mine, which is endowed with realized wisdom,
along with its esoteric secrets and its constituent parts, as it is spoken by Me."
"May you possess, through my grace, the true knowledge of me exactly as I am—my nature, my form, my qualities, and my activities.
In the beginning, I alone existed; there was nothing else, whether manifest or unmanifest, beyond me."
Afterwards, whatever this is and whatever remains— that is I.
Whatever is perceived apart from the object, yet is not perceived within the Self,
one should know that to be the Māyā of the Self, like a mirage or like darkness.
Just as the great elements enter into all beings, whether high or low, yet remain unentered within them, so too am I in relation to those things;
this alone is that which should be investigated by one who desires to know the reality of the self.
"Whatever is established through both positive and negative concomitance as being present everywhere and at all times—
abide by this doctrine with supreme concentration;
thus you shall never be deluded throughout the various cycles of cosmic ages."
Śrī Śuka said:
Having thus instructed the Parameṣṭhin among all people,
Hari, while he was looking on, withdrew His own form.
With palms joined in reverence to Hari, for whom the objects of the senses have vanished,
he who consists of all beings created this universe as before;
then Prajāpati, the Lord of Dharma, [practiced] the niyamas and yamas at one time.
Seeking the welfare of his subjects, he remained intent on his own purpose;
Nārada, his most beloved, who was devoted to him as an heir,
served him with character, humility, and self-restraint.

O King, desiring to understand the illusory power (*māyā*) of Viṣṇu, the lord of *māyā*, that great sage and supreme devotee (*mahābhāgavata*) completely satisfied his father. Observing that his father— the great-grandfather of the worlds— was pleased, [he continued].
The celestial sage (Nārada) replied: "That which you ask me, O Bhava, I shall explain.
This *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*, consisting of ten characteristics, was proclaimed by the Blessed Lord and, being pleased, the Creator of beings recited it to his son."
O King, on the bank of the Sarasvatī, Nārada spoke to the sage Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor as he was meditating upon the supreme Brahman— namely,
that which I have described to you concerning this world and the Puruṣa who arose from Vairāja.
Tell me that account as it was, along with all other questions in their entirety.
Śrī Śuka said:
Herein are described the primary creation (*sarga*), the secondary creation (*visarga*), the maintenance of the world (*sthāna*), its nourishment (*poṣaṇa*), and the divine powers (*ūtayaḥ*).
The narrations concerning the lords of the manvantaras, the cessation [of worldly existence], liberation, and the refuge—
these are described by the high-souled ones here as the characteristics of the first nine chapters for the sake of purifying the tenth, both through the words heard and their direct meaning.
The birth of the elements, the subtle elements, the senses, and the intellect is declared to be *sarga* (creation).
The *visarga* (emission) of Brahmā, resulting from the imbalance of the *guṇas*, is known as *pauruṣa* (human).
*Sthiti* (maintenance) is the victory of Vaikuṇṭha, which consists of nourishment and His grace.
The Manvantaras, the true dharma, the aids, the latent impressions of karma,
the incarnations of Hari and the deeds of His followers, and the stories of the Lord for men— all these have been proclaimed, augmented by various narratives.
The cessation of this [empirical self] along with its latent tendencies and powers is its dissolution;
liberation is the state of abiding in one's own true nature after abandoning all other forms.
Since both manifestation and cessation exist, they are determined by that [Supreme Reality].
He is the refuge, designated by the terms *paraṃ brahma* (the Supreme Brahman) and *paramātman* (the Supreme Self).
This person who is internal (*adhyātmika*) is indeed that same one who is celestial (*adhidaivika*). That person in whom both are absent is the elemental (*ādhibhautika*).
When we do not perceive any one of these three in the absence of the others,
he who knows that triad is the Self, the support of its own support.
When this Person, having split the egg, emerged from it—

Seeking a path for himself, the Pure One created the pure waters; He dwelt within those waters He had created for a thousand years. Because the waters were born from the Person (puruṣa), He is named Nārāyaṇa.
Material substance, action, time, inherent nature,
and the individual soul exist by His grace and cease to exist by His neglect;
He alone, desiring multiplicity, has arisen from the couch of yoga.
The Lord, by means of his illusory power (*māyā*), emitted his golden virility in three ways:
as pertaining to the divine (*adhidaiva*), the self (*adhyātma*), and the elemental (*adhibhūta*). Now hear how that singular virility of the Puruṣa was divided into three.
From the space within the body of the Puruṣa as he moved, there arose *ojas*, *sahas*, and *bala*; from that came the *prāṇa*, the great *asu*.
It is the *prāṇa* that all the vital breaths follow when it breathes among all living beings.
The followers breathe out after Him as they do for a king;
hunger and thirst arise within the Lord because He draws in the vital breath (prāṇa).
While He was desiring to drink and eat, the mouth was manifested first.
From the mouth, the palate was pierced, and there the tongue was produced;
from that, the various tastes were born, which are perceived by the tongue. From the mouth of the Infinite One who desired to speak, fire arose, and from those two, speech was uttered.
As he remained submerged in the water for a very long time,
his nostrils were pierced while the wind was blowing violently;
there, the wind that carries fragrance became the sense of smell within the nose of him who desired to perceive odors.

When he desired to see the Self within himself, which was devoid of light, his two eyes were pierced; thus, through the light, there arose the perception of the objects of sight. This occurred as he, being instructed by the sages, sought to grasp that very Self.
The two ears were pierced, and the sense of hearing, which perceives qualities, arose from the quarters;
as he desired to grasp the softness, hardness, lightness, heaviness, heat, and cold of objects,
the skin was pierced, and from it grew the trees of body hair.
Therein, the internal and external air, having acquired its quality through the skin, was enclosed;
then his two hands grew forth from the desire to perform various actions.
Of those two, Indra became the powerful faculty of grasping, which depends upon both.
For Him who desired to attain the goal of His choice, two feet grew forth;
from those feet, Yajña himself was produced, by whose ritual acts oblations are offered by men. For Him who sought progeny, bliss, and immortality, the organ of generation indeed burst forth.
The generative organ was formed for the sake of desires; it is the locus of both pleasure and procreation.
As he desired to cast out the impurities of the bodily elements, the anus was indeed split open. From that came the rectum, and from it Mitra; the act of excretion is the locus of both.
As he desired to create cities, the lower breath (apāna) emerged from the navel-gate of the city;
from that apāna came death, which brings about the separation of the two [the self and the body].
As he desired to obtain food and drink, the stomach, intestines, and channels were produced.
The rivers and oceans are the satisfaction and nourishment of those two, for they are dependent upon them.
As he meditated deeply upon his own *māyā*, his heart was pierced;
from that, the mind, the moon, volition, and desire emerged.
The seven constituents—skin, flesh, blood, fat, marrow, bone, and skin—are composed of earth, water, and fire; the vital breath consists of ether, water, and air;
the senses are of the nature of the qualities (guṇas), and the qualities arise from the principle of ego (bhūtādi).
The mind, whose nature consists of all modifications, and the intellect, whose form is discernment— this is the gross form of the Blessed One that has been described by me to you,
which is externally enveloped by the eight coverings beginning with the earth.
Beyond this is that which is most subtle, unmanifest, and devoid of attributes;
without beginning, middle, or end, it is eternal and beyond the reach of speech and mind. These two forms of the Blessed Lord have indeed been described by me to you.

The wise do not grasp either of these two, which are created by *māyā*. The Supreme Lord, assuming the form of Brahman, sustains names, forms, and actions through the relationship of the signified and the signifier; though he is beyond action, he appears as one possessing action.
The Prajāpatis, Manus, gods, ṛṣis, and the various classes of ancestors;
the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Asuras, and Guhyakas;
the Kinnaras, Apsarases, Nāgas, serpents, Kiṃpuruṣas, and humans.
O King, [he destroys] the Mātṛs, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Pretas, Bhūtas, Vināyakas,
Kūṣmāṇḍas, Unmādas, Vetālas, Yātudhānas, and Grahas;
as well as birds, wild animals, domestic beasts, trees, mountains, and reptiles.
Those who dwell in water, on land, and in the sky are of two kinds and four kinds;
these are the destinations of actions— wholesome, unwholesome, and mixed—
and they consist of the three qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, corresponding to gods, humans, and denizens of hell.

Even there, O King, each of these goals is further divided into three types when one particular nature is obstructed by the others. He alone is the sustainer of this world, the Blessed One who assumes the form of dharma.
Sustaining the universe by means of animals, humans, gods, and others, He maintains it;
then, as the soul of the fire of time (Kālāgnirudra), He withdraws at the appointed time this creation of His own, just as the wind disperses a mass of clouds.
The Blessed One, the most exalted of all blessed beings, has been described in this manner;
for the wise are not able to perceive the Supreme through such a description.
Nor do His activities, such as birth and so forth, conform to those of any other being.
That [agency] is indeed superimposed by *māyā* for the purpose of negating true agency; however,
this is described as the "kalpa of Brahmā" which is characterized by conceptual differentiation (*savikalpa*),
wherein the rules are common and the creations are both primary (*prākṛta*) and modified (*vaikṛta*).
I shall explain later the measurement of time, characterized by the Kalpas, as well as the Padma-kalpa; now listen. Śaunaka said:
O Sūta, as you have related how the Kṣattṛ, that most excellent devotee of the Lord,

wandered over the sacred fords of the earth after abandoning his kinsmen who were so difficult to give up; [now tell us] of the conversation between him and the son of Kuśārava, which was centered upon the supreme self.
Or rather, that Blessed One, being questioned by him, spoke the truth to him.
O gentle one, tell us this very conduct of Vidura—
the reason for his abandonment of kinsmen and how he returned once more.
Sūta said:
O kings, listen as I relate that which the great sage spoke when questioned by King Parīkṣit, in accordance with the king's inquiry.
